messages.content: I want to design an SSD-backed key-value store that limits write amplification under long-lived snapshots without sacrificing crash consistency. The target is to reduce total host-written bytes by 30% versus leveled LSM compaction under identical update-heavy workloads. It must also preserve snapshot isolation and acknowledged writes across crashes, while keeping p99 reads within 10% of baseline.

That sets a combined design goal, not just a write-reduction goal. The comparison is total host-written bytes against leveled LSM compaction under identical update-heavy workloads, with a target of 30% fewer bytes. At the same time, the store must preserve snapshot isolation and writes it has acknowledged across crashes, and its p99 read performance must remain within 10% of baseline. A design that improves writes but misses any of those other conditions would not meet the brief.
What makes the long-lived snapshots important here?

A long-lived snapshot means an older view may need to remain available while updates continue. That makes it important to consider write behavior without assuming older data can simply be discarded. The goal is to limit write amplification in that setting while still preserving snapshot isolation; it does not specify a particular mechanism for retaining or reclaiming data.
So should I treat the 30% as a reduction in all bytes written by the host, rather than just bytes associated with one background activity?

Yes. The stated measure is *total host-written bytes*. Reducing the writes from one activity would help only insofar as it brings that total down by 30% relative to leveled LSM compaction under the identical update-heavy workload. The target is not limited to a selected category of writes.
Could you put the percentage comparison in simple terms?

If leveled LSM compaction produced 100 units of total host-written bytes for a given workload, a 30% reduction would mean 70 units for that same workload. Those numbers are just an illustration of the percentage, not a measured result or a specified workload size.
Does that tell us how many bytes the SSD physically writes internally?

No. The specified comparison is host-written bytes—the writes attributed to the host side of the storage interface. It does not state a target for the SSD’s internal physical writes. The motivation is to limit write amplification, but the numerical success criterion here is specifically the total host-written-byte reduction.
What exactly has to survive a crash?

Writes that the store has acknowledged must remain preserved across crashes. That durability requirement sits alongside snapshot isolation: recovering from a crash must not come at the cost of losing acknowledged writes or abandoning the required isolation guarantee. The brief does not prescribe a particular recovery method.
Could the design acknowledge writes earlier if doing so reduced the bytes written?

Only if it can still preserve every acknowledged write across crashes. A write-saving approach cannot redefine an acknowledged write as expendable after a crash. The durability condition is a constraint on the design, not a trade-off that the 30% target permits it to relax.
And snapshot isolation cannot be weakened just because snapshots are long-lived?

Correct. Long-lived snapshots are the setting in which the store needs to limit write amplification, not an exception to snapshot isolation. The design needs to maintain the required consistent snapshot views while pursuing the host-written-byte reduction.
How should I read the p99 condition?

It constrains read performance at the 99th percentile, not merely typical reads. If p99 is being expressed as read latency, keeping it within 10% of baseline means it cannot be more than 10% slower than that baseline. The brief gives a percentage bound but no particular latency value.
Could excellent average read performance make up for a p99 result outside that bound?

Not under the stated requirement. Average performance would not replace the p99 read condition. Likewise, meeting the p99 condition would not replace the 30% host-written-byte target or the snapshot-isolation and crash-durability guarantees.
Is there an implementation strategy already implied by these targets?

No particular implementation is specified. The targets define what an SSD-backed key-value store must accomplish under long-lived snapshots: lower total host-written bytes than leveled LSM compaction by 30% on identical update-heavy workloads, preserve snapshot isolation and acknowledged writes across crashes, and keep p99 reads within 10% of baseline. They leave the mechanism open.

Let’s consider a concrete design direction: isolate snapshot-pinned versions in indexed immutable segments, compact active versions, fsync the WAL before acknowledging writes, and atomically publish manifests.

That proposal separates two concerns that can otherwise interfere with each other. Snapshot-pinned versions would be retained in indexed immutable segments, while compaction would focus on active versions. The WAL fsync before acknowledgment addresses the durability of acknowledged writes, and atomic manifest publication addresses how a new storage layout becomes visible. These are proposed mechanisms, not yet evidence that the write and read targets will be met.
Why isolate the versions pinned by snapshots instead of treating them like the active versions?

A snapshot-pinned version must remain available for the snapshot that needs it. Isolating those versions is intended to avoid repeatedly carrying them through compaction work aimed at active versions. The segments are immutable so their contents need not be rewritten merely because active versions are compacted. Whether that yields enough reduction in total writes remains to be evaluated.
Is the proposal to stop compacting altogether?

No. It explicitly calls for compacting active versions. The distinction is between versions retained for snapshots and versions in the active compaction path; it is not a proposal to eliminate compaction from the store.
What does the index contribute if the pinned segments are immutable?

Immutability describes how the segments are maintained; the index addresses how their contents can be found. Keeping pinned versions out of active compaction is useful only if reads that need those versions can still locate them. The proposal says the segments are indexed, but it does not prescribe an index format or claim a measured read cost.
So the index is relevant to the read-performance constraint, not just to write amplification?

Yes. Isolating retained versions could save rewriting, but those versions still have to be accessible to reads. Indexing is the proposed way to support that access. It does not, by itself, establish that p99 reads stay within the required bound; that remains a constraint on the design.
When you say ‘active versions,’ are you specifying an exact rule for deciding when a version moves into a pinned segment?

No exact transition rule is specified here. The proposal distinguishes snapshot-pinned versions, which are isolated in indexed immutable segments, from active versions, which are compacted. It does not define the point at which a version is classified as pinned, how a segment is populated, or when retained space can be reclaimed.
How do the WAL and manifests fit into the crash-consistency side of the idea?

They address different parts of it. Fsyncing the WAL before acknowledging a write is the proposed safeguard for that acknowledged write across a crash. Atomically publishing manifests is the proposed safeguard against exposing a partially published change to the store’s recorded layout. The proposal states both requirements without specifying a complete recovery algorithm.
Does ‘before acknowledgment’ mean the WAL fsync can happen after I’m told the write succeeded?

No. The order is explicit: the WAL must be fsynced *before* the write is acknowledged. Moving the fsync after acknowledgment would change the proposal and would leave the stated protection for acknowledged writes unestablished.
And what is being published atomically in the manifest?

The manifest represents the storage layout being made visible. Atomic publication means that publication is treated as a single change rather than exposing only part of a layout update. The proposal does not specify the manifest’s fields or the mechanism used to make publication atomic.
Would atomic manifest publication alone make acknowledged writes durable?

No; the proposal assigns that role to fsyncing the WAL before acknowledgment. Atomic manifest publication concerns layout visibility. Both are included because protecting acknowledged writes and avoiding a partially published layout are distinct crash-consistency concerns.
What if a crash happens while a new manifest is being published?

The intended property is that the manifest publication is atomic, so a partial publication is not treated as the visible layout. The proposal does not spell out the recovery procedure or every possible crash point, so it would be premature to claim a fully verified crash-recovery behavior from this description alone.
I don’t want the immutable segments to be mistaken for a claim that their contents can never become unnecessary.

That distinction matters. ‘Immutable’ says a segment is not modified in place; it does not say every version in it must be retained forever. The proposal is to isolate versions while snapshots pin them. It leaves any policy for determining when they are no longer needed unspecified.
Does this direction already demonstrate the required reduction in host-written bytes?

No. It gives a reason the reduction might be possible: pinned versions could avoid repeated rewriting while active versions continue to be compacted. It supplies no measurements, workload results, or proof that the required reduction has been achieved.
Then what is the most precise way to describe the design at this point?

It is a proposed SSD-backed key-value-store layout and publication approach: keep snapshot-pinned versions in indexed immutable segments, compact active versions, fsync the WAL before acknowledging writes, and atomically publish manifests. Its purpose is to limit rewriting under long-lived snapshots while protecting crash consistency, without assuming the performance requirements have already been demonstrated.
For the snapshot-pinned versions, what pinning granularity reduces copied bytes without pushing p99 point reads beyond 110% of the leveled LSM baseline?

That remains an open design question. Pinning granularity is the size of the unit treated as retained because a snapshot needs data within it. The aim is to avoid copying more bytes than necessary while ensuring p99 point-read latency is no greater than 110% of the leveled LSM baseline. Nothing specified so far identifies a granularity that satisfies both conditions.
When you say ‘unit,’ do you mean an individual version, or could it be a larger group?

Either illustrates the question. A fine granularity could distinguish individual needed versions from nearby versions; a coarser one could treat a larger group as pinned. Those are conceptual possibilities, not a selection of a storage format or a claim about which performs better.
How could granularity affect copied bytes?

If the pinned unit includes data a snapshot does not actually need, treating the whole unit as pinned could retain or move more data than necessary. Finer pinning might distinguish that data more precisely. But fewer copied bytes do not follow automatically from finer units: the answer depends on how the units interact with the proposed isolation of snapshot-pinned versions and compaction of active versions. The question asks which granularity works, rather than asserting one.
Then why not make the unit as small as possible?

Because copied bytes are only one side of the question. Point reads must still find the right version, including when that version is in an indexed immutable segment. A granularity that helps avoid copying could have a different read-access cost. The supplied information does not establish how that cost changes or whether the smallest possible unit would keep p99 point reads within the limit.
Is the read condition about all reads, or specifically point reads?

This question specifically names **p99 point reads**. Its threshold is 110% of the leveled LSM baseline. It does not give a separate threshold here for another read type, nor does it say that an improvement in average reads can compensate for exceeding the point-read p99 limit.
Does 110% mean a 110% increase over baseline?

No. It means 110% *of* the baseline: at most 1.10 times the baseline p99 point-read value, or 10% above it. For example, if the baseline were 100 units of read latency, the limit would be 110 units. That is an illustration of the ratio, not an observed latency.
Would exactly 110% be beyond the limit?
No. ‘Without pushing ... beyond 110%’ allows a value at 110% and excludes one above it, assuming p99 is measured as latency, where a larger value means a slower read.
Could we answer the granularity question just by counting how many versions are pinned?

Not from that count alone. The question concerns **copied bytes** and **p99 point reads**. A count of pinned versions does not, by itself, determine either the number of bytes copied or the point-read tail latency. It may describe part of the situation, but it cannot identify the requested granularity on its own.
I want to make sure ‘copied bytes’ doesn’t silently become the entire write target.

It should not. This question focuses on copied bytes as a consideration in choosing pinning granularity. The broader store goal concerns total host-written bytes, which is not necessarily identical to copied bytes. A granularity that reduces copying would not, on that fact alone, establish the broader write reduction.
Would isolating pinned versions in indexed immutable segments settle the point-read part?

No. The index provides a way for reads to locate retained versions, but its existence does not supply a p99 result. The granularity question still asks whether the arrangement reduces copying *and* keeps p99 point reads at or below 110% of the leveled LSM baseline.
Can we name the best granularity now, even provisionally?

There is no basis here to name one. We can state the trade-off being asked about—how precisely snapshot-pinned data is retained versus the resulting copied bytes and p99 point-read cost—but no candidate granularity has been shown to satisfy the 110% bound while reducing copied bytes.
My working hypothesis is that, under hour-long snapshots, 4-MiB version-segment pinning cuts host-written bytes by at least 30% versus leveled LSM, with p99 reads at no more than 1.10 times baseline.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis about pinning granularity, not a measured result. It names 4-MiB version segments, hour-long snapshots, a reduction of at least 30% in host-written bytes relative to leveled LSM, and a p99 read ceiling of 1.10× baseline. Both the write reduction and the read ceiling would need to hold for the hypothesis as stated.
Does ‘4-MiB’ describe the proposed pinning unit rather than the size of each key or value?
Yes. It describes the proposed version-segment pinning granularity. It does not specify a key size, value size, or number of versions per segment.
And MiB is deliberate here, not an interchangeable way to write MB?
Right. Four mebibytes is 4 × 2²⁰ bytes, or 4,194,304 bytes. That is the size named in the hypothesis; changing it to four decimal megabytes would change the quantity.
What does the hour-long snapshot condition contribute to the claim?

It limits the setting in which the hypothesis predicts those outcomes. The claim is about hour-long snapshots; it does not establish the same write reduction or read bound for snapshots of other durations.
Does ‘at least 30%’ mean the hypothesis fails if the reduction is exactly 30%?
No. Exactly 30% satisfies ‘at least 30%.’ A larger reduction would also satisfy that part of the hypothesis; a smaller reduction would not.
Could you express the write comparison as a ratio?

Under the same comparison, the hypothesis predicts total host-written bytes at no more than 0.70 times those of leveled LSM. For illustration, if leveled LSM wrote 100 units, 70 or fewer units would meet the stated reduction. That example expresses the threshold, not an observed result.
Why say ‘host-written bytes’ rather than just ‘copied bytes’?

Because the hypothesis makes a claim about host-written bytes overall. Pinning granularity may be relevant to how much data is copied, but reducing copied bytes alone would not prove a reduction of at least 30% in total host-written bytes.
How should I interpret the p99 half of the hypothesis?

It predicts that the p99 read value is no greater than 1.10 times its baseline value. If that value is read latency, the ceiling permits at most a 10% increase over baseline. It is a tail-read constraint, not a statement about average reads.
Is that baseline the leveled LSM baseline in the pinning-granularity question?
Yes. In this context, the baseline for the p99 read comparison is the leveled LSM baseline. The hypothesis uses leveled LSM explicitly for host-written bytes and the established baseline for reads.
Does a p99 result equal to 1.10× baseline meet the hypothesis?
Yes. The read condition is ‘≤1.10× baseline,’ so equality meets it. A result greater than 1.10× would not meet that condition, even if host-written bytes fell by more than 30%.
Conversely, could especially fast reads compensate for a 25% reduction in host-written bytes?
No. The hypothesis combines two separate thresholds. A 25% reduction would fall short of the predicted reduction of at least 30%, regardless of how favorable the p99 read result was.
Does proposing 4-MiB segments mean we have established that this is the optimal pinning granularity?

No. The hypothesis predicts that this particular granularity meets the stated write and read bounds under hour-long snapshots. It does not claim that 4 MiB is optimal, or that other granularities have been compared.
Can I infer a particular segment index or lookup procedure from the 4-MiB figure?

No. The figure specifies a pinning granularity, not an index format or a lookup procedure. The proposed indexed immutable segments provide design context, but the hypothesis does not add implementation details about how reads locate a version.
Does the hypothesis itself say anything new about crash recovery?

No. Its predictions concern host-written bytes and p99 reads under hour-long snapshots. The store still has the separate requirement to preserve snapshot isolation and acknowledged writes across crashes, but this hypothesis does not demonstrate those properties or replace the proposed WAL and manifest safeguards.
So what is the careful one-sentence version?

Under hour-long snapshots, the hypothesis is that 4-MiB version-segment pinning yields at least 30% fewer total host-written bytes than leveled LSM while keeping p99 reads at or below 1.10× the leveled LSM baseline; neither outcome is asserted as observed.
Let’s benchmark 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB snapshot-pinned segments against leveled LSM under hour-long snapshots, comparing host-written bytes and p99 reads.

That gives us a plan for comparing three pinning granularities with the leveled LSM baseline. For each of the 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB segment sizes, the planned comparison concerns total host-written bytes and p99 reads under hour-long snapshots. It is a benchmark to run, not a report of results.
Why include all three segment sizes?

They let the benchmark compare different snapshot-pinning granularities rather than examining only one. The plan does not assume which size will write fewer bytes or have the better p99 read result. Including 4 MiB also lets the proposed granularity be examined alongside a smaller and a larger one.
Should I read 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB as sizes of the snapshot-pinned segments?
Yes. Those are the three snapshot-pinned segment sizes to benchmark. They do not specify key sizes, value sizes, or how many versions a segment contains.
And is leveled LSM a fourth segment size?
No. Leveled LSM is the comparison baseline. The three segment sizes are the candidate pinning granularities being compared against it.
What exactly are we comparing on the write side?

Host-written bytes. That is broader than counting only bytes copied while handling pinned versions. The benchmark plan calls for comparing the host-written-byte totals for the three segment sizes with the leveled LSM baseline.
Does the benchmark plan already tell us whether the 4-MiB hypothesis reaches the 30% reduction?

No. The plan says to make the comparison; it supplies no measured byte counts or percentage reductions. The 30% figure can be used to interpret a result when one exists, but it is not a result of writing down the benchmark.
What is the read-side comparison?
P99 reads: the comparison concerns the read-performance tail, rather than only an average. The plan does not provide p99 values or say which segment size will have the lowest one.
The granularity question mentioned p99 point reads. Does this plan explicitly say ‘point reads’?

Its wording says ‘p99 reads’; it does not explicitly identify the read type. The granularity question is specifically about p99 point reads, so that distinction matters when interpreting whether the benchmark answers it. I would not treat an unspecified p99 read measure as a measured point-read result.
How does the 110% limit fit with the planned comparison?

The planned p99 comparison would provide the values needed to assess a read result against 110% of the leveled LSM baseline, if the p99 measure is the one required for that limit. A value at 1.10× baseline would be within the limit; one above it would not. The plan itself reports neither value.
Does ‘under hour-long snapshots’ apply to every comparison here?

Yes. Hour-long snapshots define the setting for the planned benchmark of the 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB snapshot-pinned segments against leveled LSM. This plan does not make a comparison for other snapshot durations.
If one size had fewer host-written bytes, would that automatically make it the answer?

Not by itself. The plan compares both host-written bytes and p99 reads because the granularity question has a read-performance bound as well as a write objective. A write-side advantage alone would not establish that p99 reads remain within the required limit.
Could the benchmark establish crash consistency too?

Not from the comparisons specified here. This plan measures host-written bytes and p99 reads; it does not specify a crash-consistency assessment. Preserving snapshot isolation and acknowledged writes across crashes remains a requirement, but neither property follows from these two performance comparisons.
So the benchmark is meant to inform the pinning-granularity choice, not announce one now?

Exactly. The proposed next step is to benchmark 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB snapshot-pinned segments against leveled LSM under hour-long snapshots and compare host-written bytes and p99 reads. It leaves the outcome—and any choice based on that outcome—open.
Run UpdateBench-60 with 80% updates and hour-long snapshots. Compare 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB snapshot-pinned segments against leveled LSM, and measure host-written bytes and p99 reads.

That defines the activity: run UpdateBench-60 under its stated 80%-update, hour-long-snapshot conditions, comparing each of the three segment sizes with leveled LSM on host-written bytes and p99 reads. It specifies what to measure, not any measured outcome.
Should I interpret the ‘60’ in UpdateBench-60 as the snapshot duration?

No duration is defined by the benchmark name here. The snapshot duration is stated separately as hour-long. ‘UpdateBench-60’ is the name of the workload to run; the supplied description does not explain what the number in its name denotes.
And the 80% figure refers to updates in the workload?
Yes. UpdateBench-60 is specified here with 80% updates. That describes the update-heavy condition for this activity, but it does not specify the composition of the remaining 20%.
Is leveled LSM being measured in the same benchmark, or is it just a reference from elsewhere?

The activity calls for comparing the 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB segment configurations against leveled LSM in UpdateBench-60 under hour-long snapshots. Leveled LSM is the baseline for this comparison; it is not another snapshot-pinned segment size.
What should ‘host-written bytes’ cover in this run?

The requested measure is total host-written bytes, rather than only bytes copied during a particular operation. That lets the write-side comparison address the stated host-write objective. The activity does not give a measured total for any configuration.
Do we also measure p99 reads for every segment size?

Yes. Both host-written bytes and p99 reads are to be measured for the 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB configurations and compared with leveled LSM. The two measures matter together: a reduction in host-written bytes would not, by itself, establish that read-tail performance stays within its bound.
Does ‘p99 reads’ here explicitly mean p99 point reads?

The activity says ‘p99 reads’ without explicitly specifying point reads. The pinning-granularity question concerns p99 point reads, so that distinction should remain visible: we should not claim a point-read result unless the read measure actually corresponds to point reads.
How would this run relate to the 4-MiB prediction?

It is set up to evaluate that prediction under hour-long snapshots by measuring the 4-MiB configuration against leveled LSM on host-written bytes and p99 reads. Including 1- and 16-MiB configurations also permits a comparison across the three proposed granularities. None of those comparisons has an outcome in the activity description.
Would I be justified in saying the 4-MiB configuration achieves at least 30% fewer host-written bytes because the run is specified?

No. Specifying the run does not establish its result. The at-least-30% reduction is a threshold to assess against the measured host-written-byte comparison, not a number the activity has already produced.
Same for p99 reads being at or below 1.10 times baseline?

Exactly. The p99 read bound can be assessed once the relevant measurements exist. The instruction to measure p99 reads does not itself show that the 4-MiB configuration—or either of the other sizes—meets that bound.
Do hour-long snapshots mean the whole benchmark lasts exactly one hour?
Not necessarily. ‘Hour-long’ describes the snapshots in the specified workload. The activity does not state the total benchmark runtime, so the two should not be equated.
Can we use this activity to claim acknowledged writes survive crashes?

No. Its stated measurements are host-written bytes and p99 reads. It does not describe a crash test or a snapshot-isolation check. Those guarantees remain requirements for the store, but this activity alone does not establish them.
So what do we actually have to do, without assuming any outcome?

Run UpdateBench-60 with 80% updates and hour-long snapshots; compare the 1-, 4-, and 16-MiB snapshot-pinned segment configurations against leveled LSM; and measure host-written bytes and p99 reads for that comparison. Any performance conclusion must wait for the measurements.
The UpdateBench-60 results are in: with 4-MiB pinning, host-written bytes were 68 GiB, versus 100 GiB for leveled LSM. P99 reads were 1.08× the leveled LSM baseline.

For that UpdateBench-60 comparison, the 4-MiB configuration wrote 32 GiB fewer host-written bytes than leveled LSM: 68 GiB versus 100 GiB. That is a 32% reduction relative to the 100-GiB baseline. The reported p99 read value was 108% of baseline. These are results for the stated run, not figures for every workload or snapshot duration.
Does the 32% use leveled LSM’s 100 GiB as the denominator?
Yes. The difference is 100 GiB minus 68 GiB, or 32 GiB. Dividing that difference by leveled LSM’s 100 GiB gives 0.32, or 32%.
Could I instead describe the write result as a ratio?
Yes: the 4-MiB configuration wrote 0.68× as many host-written bytes as leveled LSM in this comparison. That expresses the same 68-GiB-to-100-GiB result.
And 1.08× p99 reads means 8% above baseline, not 8% below it?
Correct. A value of 1.08× baseline is 108% of baseline, or 8% above it. No absolute p99 read value is provided.
Does that ratio say every individual read took 8% longer?
No. It describes the reported p99 read measure relative to baseline. It does not give the distribution of individual reads or say that each read changed by the same amount.
Remind me what conditions attach to these numbers.
They come from UpdateBench-60, specified with 80% updates and hour-long snapshots. The figures reported here are for its 4-MiB pinning configuration compared with leveled LSM under those conditions.
Do we have results for the 1-MiB and 16-MiB configurations too?

Not in the evidence given here. Although those sizes were included in the benchmark activity, this result supplies host-written bytes and p99 reads only for 4-MiB pinning relative to leveled LSM. It does not establish how the three sizes compare with one another.
Can the 68 GiB tell us how many bytes were copied specifically because of compaction?
No. The 68 GiB is the reported host-written-byte total for the 4-MiB configuration. There is no breakdown here assigning those bytes to compaction or any other activity.
Nor does it tell us the SSD’s internal physical write total?
Right. The measured quantity stated here is host-written bytes, not physical bytes written inside the SSD. The two should not be presented as the same measurement.
Does this result establish that acknowledged writes survived crashes during the run?
No crash outcome is reported. The evidence concerns host-written bytes and p99 reads; it does not report a crash-recovery or snapshot-isolation result.
What is the narrowest accurate statement I can make from the evidence?

In UpdateBench-60 with 80% updates and hour-long snapshots, 4-MiB pinning wrote 68 GiB of host-written bytes compared with leveled LSM’s 100 GiB—a 32% reduction—and its reported p99 reads were 1.08× the leveled LSM baseline.
I’m selecting 4-MiB snapshot-pinned segments. UpdateBench-60 met the write-byte reduction target, with p99 reads below the 1.10× limit.

That is the decision and its stated basis: use 4-MiB snapshot-pinned segments because, in UpdateBench-60, the write-byte reduction target was met and p99 reads stayed below 1.10× the leveled LSM baseline. The decision is grounded in that benchmark result; it does not assert the same outcome for every workload.
Should I describe 4 MiB as the chosen pinning granularity?
Yes. The selection is of 4-MiB snapshot-pinned segments, so 4 MiB is the chosen segment pinning granularity. It is not a statement about key size, value size, or the size of every write.
What exactly is the write-side reason for selecting it?

UpdateBench-60 met the write-byte reduction target for this choice. That target concerns total host-written bytes relative to leveled LSM, rather than just one category of copied bytes. The decision does not need a claim about which particular write activity accounted for the reduction.
And is the read-side reason that p99 reads were merely at the limit?
No. The decision says p99 reads were *below* the 1.10× limit. ‘Below’ is stricter than ‘at or below’: it places the reported p99 read comparison under 110% of the leveled LSM baseline.
Does the decision mean p99 reads improved relative to leveled LSM?

Not necessarily. Being below 1.10× baseline means they stayed within the specified ceiling; it does not, by itself, mean they were faster than baseline. The reason for selection is that the read constraint was respected while the write-byte target was met.
Am I claiming that 4 MiB is the best possible segment size?

No. Selecting 4-MiB snapshot-pinned segments on the stated UpdateBench-60 results does not establish global optimality. The decision identifies a choice that met the stated write target and read limit in that benchmark, not the best granularity under every criterion or condition.
Should the choice be described as conditional on hour-long snapshots?

The cited UpdateBench-60 comparison was conducted under hour-long snapshots, so that condition belongs with the evidence behind the selection. The decision does not establish how this pinning granularity performs with snapshots of other durations.
Does selecting these segments also establish crash consistency?

No. The stated reasons for this selection are the write-byte result and the p99 read result. Snapshot isolation and preserving acknowledged writes across crashes remain requirements, but this decision does not claim that the performance benchmark verified either property.
Could I say the read result specifically proves the p99 point-read condition?

The decision says ‘p99 reads’ without specifying point reads. It supports the stated p99-read comparison below 1.10×, but it should not be relabeled as a point-read-specific result unless that is what the reported measure covers.
What is a concise way to record the choice without overstating it?
Select 4-MiB snapshot-pinned segments: in UpdateBench-60, this configuration met the host-written-byte reduction target and kept p99 reads below 1.10× the leveled LSM baseline.
Next, implement the selected 4-MiB pinning and run CrashBench-4M. Use power-cut injections around WAL fsync and manifest publication, checking acknowledged writes and snapshot isolation.

That activity pairs the selected 4-MiB pinning implementation with a crash-consistency check. CrashBench-4M will inject power cuts around WAL fsync and manifest publication, then check whether acknowledged writes are preserved and snapshot isolation holds. This describes the work to perform, not a completed implementation or a passing test result.
Why focus the power cuts on those two points?

They are the two crash-sensitive boundaries named in the proposal. WAL fsync is tied to the rule that a write is fsynced before acknowledgment; manifest publication is tied to making a storage layout visible atomically. Injecting power cuts around them is intended to examine the guarantees at those boundaries, rather than infer crash consistency from the write and read benchmark.
Does the activity require us to change the selected segment size during the crash test?
No. It says to implement the selected 4-MiB pinning and run CrashBench-4M on that basis. It does not call for a new pinning-granularity comparison.
For the WAL check, which writes matter to the stated guarantee?

The explicit durability check concerns **acknowledged writes**: writes the store has reported as accepted must be preserved across a power cut. The activity does not specify a required outcome for writes that had not been acknowledged.
If a cut occurs close to the fsync, can we treat every write in progress as acknowledged?

No. Proximity to fsync does not itself tell us whether a write was acknowledged. The check needs to distinguish the acknowledgment boundary from the power-cut point so that it assesses the stated guarantee without assuming an in-progress write had been acknowledged.
What is the manifest-publication part meant to check?

It targets the proposal to publish manifests atomically. Power cuts around publication provide a way to check that recovery does not expose a partially published layout in a way that breaks the required guarantees. The activity does not prescribe the publication mechanism or report what the injections find.
Could passing the acknowledged-write check alone settle the snapshot question?

No. Preserving acknowledged writes and preserving snapshot isolation are both explicit checks. A durable set of acknowledged writes would not, by itself, show that snapshots retain their required consistent views across the injected power cuts.
Is snapshot isolation only relevant when the power cut happens during a read?

The activity does not limit its snapshot-isolation check to a particular operation in progress. It asks whether snapshot isolation is preserved under the power-cut injections around WAL fsync and manifest publication. We should not narrow that check to cuts during reads without such a condition being specified.
